extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and science policy makers; journal editors and other stakeholders concerned with peer-review design and bias
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing sources and magnitudes of disagreement and favoritism in scientific peer review (using co-authorship networks and reviewer outcomes), and evaluating policy responses (blinding, recusal, reviewer diversity, editorial selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity as sole review criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS ONE evaluates manuscripts only on whether claims are valid (i.e., scientific validity alone), with the policy designed to rule out subjective review criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review process was designed specifically with this goal in mind; if followed, it should rule out subjective criteria. Nevertheless reviewers may fail to comply with instructions. The paper finds that even under a validity-only regime, disagreement and favoritism persist, suggesting limitations to this policy as a means to eliminate subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (measure of reviewer disagreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-rater reliability quantifies how often reviewers agree; reported inter-rater reliability = 0.19 for PLOS ONE reviews in this study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inter-rater reliability to compare disagreement across review systems (validity-oriented vs conventional). A low value (here, 0.19) indicates frequent disagreement similar to settings using more subjective criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-authorship proximity bias (favoritism by network distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers give authors a bonus of ~0.11 points on a 4-point scale for every increased step of co-authorship network proximity; close reviewers rarely reject (7.1%) while most distant reject >20% (20.4%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure co-authorship distance (co-author = distance 1; co-author of co-author = distance 2; 3+ further). Regression results show steadiness of increased rejection probability with distance. Interpret effects using manuscript fixed effects to compare reviewers on the same manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing nepotism from schools of thought as bias mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Two candidate mechanisms for favoritism: nepotism (favoritism for personal/self-benefit) and schools of thought (shared epistemic/methodological commitments leading to systematic favoring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nepotism is expected to be most salient in competitive/zero-sum environments and concentrated among close connections. Schools-of-thought predict smooth variation in favoritism with network proximity (distant reviewers more favorable than very distant). Evaluate evidence from acceptance policies, blinding experiments, and patterns of favoritism across distance levels to adjudicate mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding (anonymization) of author identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymizing scientific work before review is a policy intended to reduce nepotism by preventing reviewers from identifying authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomized trials of blinding have produced inconsistent results (Fisher et al., 1994; Jefferson et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2013), suggesting either reviewers can guess identities or nepotism is not the main driver. Blinding should be evaluated empirically and cannot be assumed to remove bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection trade-off: expertise versus bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing reviewers is a trade-off between (1) expert reviewers biased toward their research area (better discrimination in that area) and (2) less expert reviewers who may be less biased but less discriminating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessments of completed work with high expertise, the choice may be effectively between a 'positive' expert from inside the author's school of thought and a 'negative' expert outside it. Editors should be aware that expertise selection can inadvertently sample from large schools of thought and thus introduce bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal policies for close connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Common policy: recuse reviewers who are closely connected to authors (e.g., co-authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy is sensible under the assumption nepotism is concentrated among close reviewers. The study shows bias extends beyond close ties — distant reviewers are biased relative to more distant ones — so recusal of only closest connections may be insufficient to eliminate favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruit reviewers from diverse co-authorship clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers from the same co-authorship cluster share scientific views and favor each other's work, fair reviews require recruiting reviewers from diverse co-authorship clusters (i.e., diverse schools of thought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diverse evaluators can recognize and flag assumptions not shared across evaluators and help editors understand how substantive differences affect recommendations. This policy response emphasizes balancing evaluators to produce diversity in critiques and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compliance with review instructions as a source of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may fail to follow instructions (e.g., to judge only validity), which can reintroduce subjective criteria and nepotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be able to identify non-compliant reviewers and either train them or exclude them from future invitations. Non-compliance is distinct from structural mechanisms like schools of thought but contributes to observed disagreement and favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of reviewer outcomes (review score scale and rejection probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent variable used: Review score coded 1.0 = Reject to 4.0 = Accept; probabilities of rejection and mean scores reported as functions of co-authorship distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling reviewer behavior, clearly define outcome scale, report probabilities and mean differences, and use significance markers (e.g., *, **, ***) with standard error reporting. Use within-manuscript comparisons where possible to control manuscript quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling choices: within-manuscript fixed-effects regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Use OLS regression with manuscript fixed effects to estimate bias shown by reviewers, controlling for reviewer attributes (e.g., h-index, number of co-authorships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report within-manuscript R2, F-statistics, observations, and standard errors. Treat co-authorship distance as factor levels (distance 1 reference) to estimate favoritism at different proximity levels. Interpret coefficients as differences in score controlling for manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and measurement of co-authorship network
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-authorship network constructed using Scopus author IDs and API queries, 'one-level-out' (lifetime co-authors returned up to 179), producing ~1.82M nodes and ~4.19M edges; co-authorship distance measured between reviewer and authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of data limits: Scopus API returns up to 179 co-authors per author (creating an artificial peak), network constructed one-level-out may omit ties, and 99.59% connectivity is reported. These construction choices affect distance measurement and downstream bias estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement error in co-authorship distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing nodes and ties bias measured co-authorship distances upward, especially for distances 4+, so distances 4+ were recoded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A1 outlines expected effects of missing data: distances 1–3 are robust to missing nodes/ties, distances 4+ likely upward-biased. Researchers should account for API limits (179 co-authors) and consider recoding or sensitivity analyses to handle measurement error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and generalizability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Study limitations include focus on a single discipline (neuroscience), uniqueness of PLOS ONE (validity-oriented, non-zero-sum acceptance policy), inability to measure true manuscript quality, and models explaining only a small proportion of within-manuscript score variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in generalizing findings to other disciplines (e.g., economics) or conventional review settings. Recognize that small explained variance may result from constrained selection of reviewers by editors and that disagreement may vary by contestedness of scientific claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication: acceptance policy (non-zero-sum) effect on nepotism incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS ONE's policy of publishing any submission meeting standards of scientific validity and its relatively high acceptance rate (~70%) make it non-zero-sum and should reduce incentives for nepotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite this design, the study observes favoritism, indicating that non-zero-sum acceptance does not eliminate bias; thus policy designers should not assume reduced competition alone removes nepotistic or epistemic biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative advantage via schools of thought and reviewer sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: High-status authors tend to have more connections and thus larger schools of thought; editors choosing reviewers by expertise may unintentionally sample from large schools and solicit more favorable reviews, producing cumulative advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how reviewer selection protocols can amplify status-based advantages; to mitigate, incorporate evaluator diversity and be aware that expertise-based selection can bias outcomes toward established/successful groups.
